questions.question: What is the most useful first step when a patient says they are dizzy?
choices: Clarify whether the symptom is vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium, or nonspecific lightheadedness using timing and triggers
Assume dizziness means benign positional vertigo
Order the same imaging study for every patient
Treat the symptom without asking about onset or associated features
questions.explanation: Dizziness is a nonspecific word. A time- and trigger-based history plus associated symptoms produces a safer, more focused differential.

questions.question: Which pattern most supports benign paroxysmal positional vertigo when no red flags are present?
choices: Brief spinning episodes consistently triggered by rolling in bed or changing head position
Continuous vertigo with inability to walk and double vision
Syncope during exertion without warning
Sudden unilateral weakness with dizziness
questions.explanation: BPPV typically causes brief, reproducible position-triggered vertigo. Persistent symptoms, severe gait instability, or neurologic deficits require reassessment for central causes.

questions.question: Which finding with acute vertigo is most concerning for posterior-circulation stroke?
choices: Severe gait instability with double vision and dysarthria
A few seconds of spinning when turning in bed
Stable tinnitus without imbalance
Lightheadedness after skipping breakfast with complete rapid recovery
questions.explanation: Vertigo plus severe imbalance, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, focal symptoms, or altered consciousness can indicate posterior circulation or brainstem stroke.

questions.question: What is the correct role of the HINTS examination in dizziness evaluation?
choices: It is a specialized examination for selected continuous acute vestibular syndromes and requires correct training and application
It rules out stroke in every patient who reports dizziness
It is intended for brief intermittent positional symptoms
It replaces emergency evaluation when central signs are present
questions.explanation: HINTS is not a general dizziness screening tool. Incorrect use or use in the wrong syndrome can create false reassurance when stroke evaluation is needed.

questions.question: Which element belongs in the initial evaluation of true syncope?
choices: Detailed history, focused examination, vital signs, and a 12-lead ECG
Routine neuroimaging for every episode
A diagnosis based only on the patient’s age
No medication review if the event lasted less than one minute
questions.explanation: Guideline-based initial syncope evaluation centers on history, physical examination, heart rate and blood pressure assessment, and ECG, followed by targeted testing when indicated.

questions.question: Which syncopal event is most concerning for a cardiac cause?
choices: Sudden loss of consciousness during exertion with no prodrome
Faintness after prolonged standing with nausea and visual gray-out
Brief lightheadedness that improves after sitting in a hot room
Dizziness only during a familiar BPPV episode
questions.explanation: Exertional syncope, sudden collapse without prodrome, supine syncope, palpitations, abnormal ECG, or structural heart disease raise concern for cardiac syncope.

questions.question: Which history most supports reflex or vasovagal syncope in an otherwise low-risk patient?
choices: Prolonged standing followed by warmth, nausea, sweating, tunnel vision, and rapid recovery
Loss of consciousness while lying flat without warning
Fainting with exertion and chest discomfort
Sudden collapse followed by persistent focal weakness
questions.explanation: A situational trigger and recognizable autonomic prodrome are common in reflex syncope. Risk assessment still includes examination, ECG, injury, and comorbidities.

questions.question: Why is medication review essential in a patient with dizziness or syncope?
choices: Cumulative effects of blood-pressure medicines, diuretics, sedatives, substances, and glucose-lowering therapy can contribute to symptoms
Medication history does not affect syncope risk
All medications should be stopped immediately after a fainting episode
Only antibiotics can cause dizziness
questions.explanation: Medication effects and interactions can contribute to orthostasis, sedation, arrhythmia risk, or hypoglycemia. Changes should be individualized and coordinated safely.

questions.question: A patient with diabetes and neuropathy has a new warm swollen foot and reports imbalance. Which statement is safest?
choices: Do not anchor on dizziness alone; assess gait, neurologic signs, medications, foot pathology, and fall risk in the full clinical context
Assume all imbalance is a benign inner-ear disorder
Ignore new foot changes because they cannot affect function
Treat only with a vestibular medication without examination
questions.explanation: Dizziness and imbalance can be multifactorial. Neuropathy, foot pathology, medications, neurologic disease, and cardiovascular conditions can all affect gait and safety.

questions.question: What is the most appropriate disposition for acute vertigo with vomiting, double vision, and inability to stand without support?
choices: Emergency stroke-capable evaluation
Routine outpatient vestibular follow-up in several weeks
Home repositioning exercises without assessment
Reassurance because vertigo is always peripheral
questions.explanation: The combination of acute vestibular symptoms, diplopia, and profound gait instability is concerning for a central neurologic process and requires emergency assessment.
